source.title: Mapping the Schedule x Bit-Width Boundary in Sub-100M Quantisation-Aware Training

page_placements.theme: Precision and compression penalties depend on size and training intensity

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study investigates QAT schedule preferences and quantisation penalties, not the power-law behavior of held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its INT6 penalty fit is a different quantity from the loss scaling claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation BPB and a size-dependent INT6 quantisation penalty, including a fit and held-out prediction check. These bear on scaling-related behavior but do not test the listed versions: the fitted quantity is the INT6-minus-FP16 penalty, not held-out loss, and the study does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Schedule-preference results are not recorded because they concern warmdown choice rather than the claimed allocation or loss-scaling behavior.
record.test_reason: The study is about whether the optimal QAT learning-rate warmdown depends on bit-width. It reports validation BPB at a few sizes but fits no law to total held-out loss, runs no fixed-compute allocation sweep, has no controlled shape comparison and no downstream tasks. Its 'log-linear scaling law' is for the INT6-minus-FP16 penalty, a different quantity from loss. The originals are not cited.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but omits the main conclusion. The authors' primary result is that the optimal warmdown (33%) is bit-width-agnostic for FP16/INT8/INT6 across 15M–350M. This null holds under AdamW, cosine warmdown and 9× longer training. INT4 is noise-dominated below 50M and decisively wd33 at and above 50M. Secondary results: the INT6 penalty shrinks log-linearly with size, predicting 5/5 held-out sizes, and grows with training length. Grid-snapping is ruled out as the mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: Not a reproduction of either original scaling-law study; it studies from-initialisation weight-only QAT schedule sensitivity and quantisation penalties.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported penalty depends on model size and training length; the largest three held-out size measurements have positive residuals relative to the fit. Schedule-shape changes produce a small absolute BPB difference, but that is outside the listed claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Paired INT6−FP16 BPB penalty falls log-linearly with size (+5.85−0.89·log M). A fit on 15M–100M predicts held-out 5M–350M within the 95% PI (5/5), but the three largest residuals are positive.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In from-initialisation weight-only QAT, the INT6 quantisation penalty decreases log-linearly with model size and extrapolates across ~70×, with possible flattening at the top.

fits_no_version.finding: At 30M, the INT6 penalty grows with training length: +3.0 mBPB at 9k, +4.0 at 27k and +6.5 at 81k iterations. Size and iteration effects do not collapse onto a single compute axis.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The quantisation penalty depends on size and training length separately, growing with tokens at fixed size.

fits_no_version.finding: The INT4 penalty falls with size from +39.0 to +14.8 mBPB, with the largest drop between 30M and 50M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The INT4 QAT penalty decreases with model size, non-uniformly.

fits_no_version.finding: FP16/INT8/INT6 validation BPB decreases from 15M to 100M at fixed 9k iterations. No fit is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Descriptive only: loss decreases with size in this setup.

record.problems: The study uses one decoder-only architecture family, one tokeniser, and one dataset. The held-out size prediction validation is for the INT6-minus-FP16 penalty rather than total loss. The paper flags positive residuals at the three largest held-out sizes as a possible flattening trend. No total-loss power-law fit or fixed-compute allocation sweep is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Schedule-preference results and the weight-to-grid-distance probe were not extracted because they do not measure a quantity named by the claim versions. Other QAT ablation results were likewise left out as outside the claim’s loss-scaling and allocation subject.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss. FP16 BPB is given at only four sizes (15M–100M) at a fixed 9k iterations; it falls with size but no form is tested.
No extrapolation of total loss. The held-out prediction check (5M–350M) concerns the INT6 penalty only.
No fixed-compute sweep and no optimal N/D allocation.
Width and depth vary together with size; there is no comparison at fixed parameter count.
The QAT loss itself is not fitted. The penalty fit is log-linear, not a power law of loss.
No loss exponents or allocation fits whose setup-dependence could be assessed.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T6 gate is correct. All rows are correctly linked to none. Loss values come from fixed-iteration runs, so tokens are not scaled with size; even a fit to r1–r12 would not isolate a parameter power law.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or test of held-out loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; the reported fit is for the INT6-minus-FP16 penalty.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run held-out loss; the held-out predictions concern the INT6-minus-FP16 penalty.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is tested.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer setting is tested.
The reported fitting and residual observations concern the quantisation penalty, not exponents or compute-optimal allocation for held-out loss.

relation.reason: The study discusses related compute-optimal QAT scaling work but neither tests a listed claim version nor uses an established scaling law as a tool.

tranche.reason: The fitted relationship concerns the INT6-minus-FP16 loss penalty, rather than a power law for total held-out loss. Schedule sensitivity and penalty scaling do not test the listed claim versions.
